title: Group 2 — Risk factors
text:
Spine

How do bodies carry risk, how do class and smoke talk, and where do children still die young?



Introduction — the tables we own
This folder is ours for the ten days. Three tables, three shapes.

Panel A (panel-A.csv) — cardioRiskFactors: BMI, lipids, blood pressure, uric acid. sex and smok have already been recoded from integers to factors.
Panel B (panel-B.csv) — Scottish Health Survey 1998: sex, social class, smoking, diagnosed CVD. area is a code, not a map.
Panel C (panel-C.csv) — SOWC child / infant / neonatal mortality by country. Join by country name.

If a brick needs a histogram, it lives in A. If it needs a mosaic, it lives in B.

A few helper columns for later bricks. These are cut-offs we chose, not columns in the data: “high bp” is sys >= 140 or dia >= 90, “obese” is bmi >= 30, “drinker” is alco > 0.

  mutate(

    obese   = (bmi >= 30),
    drinker = (alco > 0)
  )

  pct_high_bp = mean(high_bp),

Findings from this look:

524 women and 474 men; 775 non-smokers and 223 smokers (only 36 women smoke, compared to 187 men).
Most people don’t drink: 721 of 998.
48% of people have high blood pressure.
20% of people are obese (bmi >= 30).



2. Ask
Based on the spine, these are our questions:
Possibly can answer:

Are women and men affected differently? Do they carry risk in different ways?
Is waisthip a better match for risk markers than bmi? (Where you carry weight vs how much.)
Do smokers and non-smokers have different hdl and ldl levels, for men and for women? Is the pattern still there for non-drinkers? (Main Character Question)

Possibly cannot answer:

How much smoking matters. (No dose or duration of smoking, just smoker / non-smoker.)
Did any of these people get heart disease? (No outcome column, so we can’t tell whether a “high” value actually leads to heart disease.)



3. Choose a mark

Bar chart for the Qual counts (sex, smok), no histograms for these.
Histograms for single Quant variables (age, bmi, sys, alco, …)
Scatter + straight-line smoother for Quant + Quant (sys ~ age, sys ~ waisthip, sys ~ bmi, hdl ~ trig, hdl ~ alco), with a correlation number to back it up
Violins for Quant + Qual (2 levels): body measures by sex, and hdl / ldl by smok, split by sex
Density plot to see hdl and ldl side by side in one chart
Two-sample test for means beside the matching violin



4. Predict

Question 1: Men will carry more weight around the middle (waisthip), even if women have the higher bmi.
Question 2: waisthip will line up with blood pressure and uric acid more closely than bmi does.
Question 3 (Main Character): Smokers will have worse cholesterol: lower hdl and higher ldl than non-smokers.



5. Make
These are the charts we used to explore the data. They don’t show up in the render, but they helped us decide what to look at next.

Question 3 (Main Character): smokers and cholesterol, men and women separately
Human brick first: our own starting chart, before any AI.

# Our first attempt: HDL and LDL as two separate graphs
A_mod |> gf_histogram(~ hdl, fill = ~ smok, position = "dodge", bins = 25) |> gf_facet_wrap(~ factor(sex))
A_mod |> gf_histogram(~ ldl, fill = ~ smok, position = "dodge", bins = 25) |> gf_facet_wrap(~ factor(sex))

Problem: two separate graphs, so it’s hard to compare HDL and LDL side by side.

# ## Prompt we actually used
# "how can I plot these 2 graphs together so I can analyse both hdl and ldl side by side"

# ai_draft
A_mod |>
  pivot_longer(c(hdl, ldl), names_to = "cholesterol", values_to = "level") |>
  gf_density(~ level, fill = ~ smok, alpha = 0.5) |>
  gf_facet_grid(cholesterol ~ factor(sex))

# ours
# kept pivot_longer() + gf_facet_grid(), tried it as a histogram first,
# switched to density because the groups are really uneven (36 vs 488 women),
# added a title + caption


A_mod |>
  pivot_longer(c(hdl, ldl), names_to = "cholesterol", values_to = "level") |>
  gf_density(~ level, fill = ~ smok, alpha = 0.5) |>
  gf_facet_grid(cholesterol ~ sex) |>
  gf_labs(
    title = "Male smokers have more good cholesterol and less bad; women barely differ",
    caption = "Panel A, cardioRiskFactors (n = 998). Only 36 women smoke.",
    x = "Cholesterol (mmol/L)"
  )

  gf_labs(title = "Male smokers have higher good cholesterol (HDL)", x = NULL,

  gf_labs(title = "Male smokers have lower bad cholesterol (LDL)", x = NULL)

  summarise(n = n(), mean_hdl = mean(hdl), mean_ldl = mean(ldl), .groups = "drop")

6. Say

Prediction missed. Male smokers have higher hdl (about 0.24 higher on average) and lower ldl (about 0.5 lower) than male non-smokers, both p-values far below 0.05.
The pattern is still there among men who don’t drink (hdl about 0.23 higher, ldl about 0.5 lower), so drinking alone doesn’t explain it. Among women the gap is small, and only 36 women smoke.
Women carry risk differently from men: higher bmi in women; higher waisthip, blood pressure and Uric in men.
Blood pressure rises with age, and waisthip lines up with the risk markers (Uric, trig, sys) more closely than bmi does.
48% of this group has high blood pressure, 20% is obese, and 721 of 998 don’t drink.



7. Limit

We can’t say how much smoking matters: we only have smoker / non-smoker, no amount or duration.
We can’t say whether anyone got heart disease. There’s no outcome column, so a “high” value can’t be turned into “more likely to get heart disease”.
“High blood pressure”, “obese” and “drinker” are cut-offs we chose, not columns in the data.
This is one sample of 998 people. Associations here are not causes: a smoker’s higher hdl is not a reason to smoke.
Only 36 women smoke, too few to be sure about women.
We don’t know who these people are, where they’re from, or how they were chosen.
ldl is calculated from choles, hdl and trig, not measured on its own.
Some values are extreme (dia up to 172, Uric up to 1885).
Kit table we refused to abuse: smok and sex were never averaged or put in a histogram.

Class and place talk: higher social classes live in less deprived areas (class I–II average carstair -1.24 vs +0.65 for class IV–V, p far below 0.05).

7. Limit

One snapshot from 1998. Links, not causes.
We don’t know when people quit smoking or when CVD was diagnosed, so some ex-smokers may have quit because they got ill.
smoke is in groups, and we don’t know what “lite” or “hvy” actually means in cigarettes.
carstair describes the area, not the person: a well-off person in a deprived area gets the area’s score.
sc is based on job type, which leaves out people without a job and says nothing about income.
cvd is just yes / no, with no type or severity.
Age affects almost everything here, and we haven’t fully separated it out.
The deprivation groups are cut-offs we chose (equal thirds).
Kit table we refused to abuse: sc and area were never averaged or treated as numbers, and area was never used as a map.

I wanted to use maps to understand the places and people connected to Erin Brockovich’s investigation. Map 1 — Households and water samples
The first map shows where the households are located and colours them according to their recorded water-sample category. The shaded polygon gives a visual reference area for comparing the household locations.








Map 2 — Household health reports
For the second map, I used the health-report categories stored in the household impacts dataset. The same household coordinates are used, but the colours now represent the recorded health categories.








Map 3 — Families who moved or stayed
The third map compares households marked as having left their property with those not marked as having moved. This connects the geographical information to the effect the investigation had on families and their homes.








Map 4 — Erin’s journey
I also wanted to show the wider geographical context of the investigation. This map connects Hinkley with an assumed home and law-firm locations in the Los Angeles area.








What I noticed
Making these maps helped me see how location adds another layer to the story. The household maps show how the same locations can be understood through different lenses. The regional map connects Hinkley to the Los Angeles area and gives a sense of the distances involved in Erin’s investigation.



Conclusion

The spine so far: Bodies carry risk differently by sex (A), class talks to where people live and how much they smoke more than to heart disease directly (B), and smoking keeps refusing to behave the way we predicted in both panels.
The questions we will defend in ninety seconds:

Panel A: Do smokers and non-smokers carry cholesterol differently, and why do male smokers look healthier?
Panel B: Does smoking lower your risk of CVD? (No: ex-smokers have the most CVD, and they’re also the oldest.)

What we will not claim: that smoking is good for cholesterol or the heart, that social class causes CVD, or that anything here causes heart disease.
Which lines were human, which were machine:

Human: the questions in both panels, the predictions, the first HDL/LDL histograms, the sys/dia scatter, using facet_wrap() by sex, spotting the “how many cigarettes” limit, the helper columns and cut-offs, the violins and tally() counts, the cholesterol-by-sex histogram and t-test from class, the carstair histogram faceted by smoke, and the smoke × cvd mosaics and chi-square test.
Machine (AI-assisted): the pivot_longer() combined chart,, formatting index.qmd into the template layout, merging drafts into one file, formatting Panel B, the deprivation groups (cut_number()), the age check for ex-smokers, and checking the numbers in both panels.

Limits: one snapshot each, smoking is yes / no only in A and in loose groups in B, only 36 female smokers in A, age tangled up with smoking in B, carstair describes the area not the person, unknown sampling.
Gift for the steal-this strip: pivot_longer() to put two measures side by side in one faceted chart, helper columns with cut-offs stated out loud, and fct_relevel() / fct_recode() to put categories in a sensible order with readable names.

Panel D — Mapping the Hinkley case
For this panel, I wanted to look at how mapping can help tell the story of the Hinkley case. Instead of only reading about the families, I plotted households in relation to the area where the groundwater contamination happened. I then used different colours to compare water-sample categories, health reports, and families who had moved or stayed.

# Install once in the RStudio Console if needed:
# install.packages(c("ggplot2", "dplyr", "readr"))

library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(readr)

households <- read_csv("data/households_simulated.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
impacts <- read_csv("data/household_impacts_simulated.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
water <- read_csv("data/water_samples_simulated.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

families <- households |>
  left_join(impacts, by = "household_id") |>
  left_join(water, by = "household_id") |>
  mutate(
    water_category = coalesce(simulated_concentration_category, "No sample category"),
    health_report = case_when(
      reported_cancer_history_simulated == "Yes" ~ "Cancer history reported",
      reported_symptoms_simulated == "Yes" ~ "Symptoms reported",
      TRUE ~ "No report in this record"
    ),
    move_status = case_when(
      property_sold_or_left_simulated == "Yes" | relocated_by_context_year_simulated == "Yes" ~ "Moved / left property",
      TRUE ~ "Stayed / not marked as moved"
    )
  )

# A simple illustrative plume shape for practicing map layers.
# It is a drawn shape, not an official boundary.
plume <- data.frame(
  x = c(-117.424, -117.407, -117.377, -117.346, -117.314, -117.302,
        -117.323, -117.354, -117.389, -117.417),
  y = c(35.101, 35.119, 35.124, 35.111, 35.087, 35.054,
        35.035, 35.030, 35.047, 35.073)
)

map_base <- function() {
  ggplot() +
    geom_polygon(data = plume, aes(x = x, y = y),
                 fill = "#f4a261", colour = "#c65d21", alpha = 0.35,
                 linewidth = 0.8) +
    coord_quickmap() +
    labs(x = "Longitude", y = "Latitude") +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
    theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
          plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"))
}


Map 1 — Households and water samples
I used colour to show the different water-sample categories. The outlined area gives a visual idea of a possible contamination zone, so it is easier to compare where the household points sit in relation to it. The shape is an illustration for the mapping exercise rather than an official plume boundary.

map_base() +
  geom_point(data = families,
             aes(x = longitude_simulated, y = latitude_simulated,
                 colour = water_category), size = 2.5, alpha = 0.9) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(
    "Higher simulated concentration" = "#b2182b",
    "Moderate simulated concentration" = "#ef8a62",
    "Lower simulated concentration" = "#2166ac",
    "No sample category" = "#777777"),
    name = "Water sample") +
  labs(title = "Households and water-sample categories",
       subtitle = "The shaded shape is an illustrative area")










Map 2 — Health reports
For the second map, I changed the colour variable to the health information recorded for each household. This makes it easier to see how the same locations can tell a different story depending on which variable is mapped. The map shows reported categories, not proof that a particular exposure caused an illness.

map_base() +
  geom_point(data = families,
             aes(x = longitude_simulated, y = latitude_simulated,
                 colour = health_report), size = 2.5, alpha = 0.9) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(
    "Cancer history reported" = "#b2182b",
    "Symptoms reported" = "#ef8a62",
    "No report in this record" = "#2166ac"),
    name = "Health report") +
  labs(title = "Household health reports",
       subtitle = "Colours show the category recorded for each household")










Map 3 — Families who moved or stayed
The third map focuses on relocation. I used two colours to compare households marked as having left a property with those not marked that way. It connects to the human side of Erin’s investigation: the issue was not only about water measurements, but also about what happened to people and their homes.

map_base() +
  geom_point(data = families,
             aes(x = longitude_simulated, y = latitude_simulated,
                 colour = move_status), size = 2.5, alpha = 0.9) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(
    "Moved / left property" = "#d73027",
    "Stayed / not marked as moved" = "#1a9850"),
    name = "Property status") +
  labs(title = "Households by relocation status",
       subtitle = "Comparing households marked as moved or stayed")










Map 4 — Erin’s journey between the case and the law firm
I also wanted to show the larger geography of the investigation. Erin’s work took her from the Los Angeles area to Hinkley, where residents were concerned about their water. For this map, I used approximate example locations for a home and a law firm so I could practise plotting places and comparing distances. The straight-line distances are only approximate and are not driving distances.

places <- data.frame(
  place = c("Hinkley — case location", "Erin's home — example location",
            "Law firm — example location"),
  longitude = c(-117.1920, -118.7745, -118.5365),
  latitude = c(35.0419, 34.1367, 34.2283),
  type = c("Case location", "Home (example)", "Law firm (example)")
)

# Haversine formula for approximate straight-line distances in kilometres.
haversine_km <- function(lon1, lat1, lon2, lat2) {
  rad <- pi / 180
  dlon <- (lon2 - lon1) * rad
  dlat <- (lat2 - lat1) * rad
  a <- sin(dlat / 2)^2 + cos(lat1 * rad) * cos(lat2 * rad) * sin(dlon / 2)^2
  6371 * 2 * atan2(sqrt(a), sqrt(1 - a))
}

places$distance_from_hinkley_km <- c(
  0,
  haversine_km(places$longitude[1], places$latitude[1], places$longitude[2], places$latitude[2]),
  haversine_km(places$longitude[1], places$latitude[1], places$longitude[3], places$latitude[3])
)

# Keep labels short so they do not overlap too much.
ggplot(places, aes(x = longitude, y = latitude, colour = type)) +
  geom_point(size = 4) +
  geom_text(aes(label = place), nudge_y = 0.06, size = 3.5, show.legend = FALSE) +

  scale_colour_manual(values = c(

text:
Panel D — Mapping Erin Brockovich’s investigation
I wanted to use maps to understand the places and people connected to Erin Brockovich’s investigation. Instead of looking at the household information only as a table, I mapped the locations to compare water samples, health reports and relocation. I also made a regional map to show the journey between Hinkley and the Los Angeles area.

households <- read_csv(
  "data/households_simulated.csv",
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

water <- read_csv(
  "data/water_samples_simulated.csv",
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

impacts <- read_csv(
  "data/household_impacts_simulated.csv",
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

families <- households |>
  left_join(
    water |>
      select(
        household_id,
        chromium_vi_ug_l_simulated,
        simulated_concentration_category,
        water_sampled_simulated
      ),
    by = "household_id"
  ) |>
  left_join(
    impacts |>
      select(
        household_id,
        reported_symptoms_simulated,
        reported_cancer_history_simulated,
        property_sold_or_left_simulated,
        water_concern_level_simulated
      ),
    by = "household_id"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    water_category = coalesce(
      as.character(simulated_concentration_category),
      "No household well sample"
    ),

    health_report = case_when(
      reported_cancer_history_simulated == "Yes" ~
        "Cancer history reported",
      reported_symptoms_simulated == "Yes" ~
        "Symptoms reported",
      TRUE ~ "No report in this record"
    ),

    movement = case_when(
      property_sold_or_left_simulated == "Yes" ~
        "Moved / left property",
      property_sold_or_left_simulated == "No" ~
        "Not marked as moved",
      TRUE ~ "Status unavailable"
    )
  ) |>
  filter(
    !is.na(longitude_simulated),
    !is.na(latitude_simulated)
  )

plume_lng <- c(
  -117.414, -117.400, -117.381, -117.360,
  -117.341, -117.326, -117.316, -117.323,
  -117.343, -117.362, -117.386, -117.405
)

plume_lat <- c(
  35.101, 35.119, 35.124, 35.112,
  35.101, 35.086, 35.064, 35.048,
  35.035, 35.030, 35.041, 35.066
)

osm_url <- "https://{s}.tile.openstreetmap.org/{z}/{x}/{y}.png"

osm_credit <- paste0(
  '© <a href="https://www.openstreetmap.org/copyright">',
  'OpenStreetMap</a> contributors'
)

make_local_map <- function() {
  leaflet() |>
    addTiles(
      urlTemplate = osm_url,
      attribution = osm_credit,
      group = "Street map"
    ) |>
    addPolygons(
      lng = plume_lng,
      lat = plume_lat,
      group = "Illustrative contamination zone",
      color = "#C64E16",
      weight = 2,
      fillColor = "#F4A261",
      fillOpacity = 0.30,
      label = "Illustrative contamination zone"
    ) |>
    addLayersControl(
      baseGroups = "Street map",
      overlayGroups = "Illustrative contamination zone",
      options = layersControlOptions(collapsed = FALSE)
    ) |>
    fitBounds(
      lng1 = -117.435,
      lat1 = 35.005,
      lng2 = -117.295,
      lat2 = 35.135
    )
}


Map 1 — Households and water samples
The first map shows where the households are located and colours them according to their recorded water-sample category. The shaded polygon gives a visual reference area for comparing the household locations.








Map 2 — Household health reports
For the second map, I used the health-report categories stored in the household impacts dataset. The same household coordinates are used, but the colours now represent the recorded health categories.








Map 3 — Families who moved or stayed
The third map compares households marked as having left their property with those not marked as having moved. This connects the geographical information to the effect the investigation had on families and their homes.








Map 4 — Erin’s journey
I also wanted to show the wider geographical context of the investigation. This map connects Hinkley with example home and law-firm locations in the Los Angeles area. The two example locations are for the mapping exercise rather than verified historical addresses.








What I noticed
Making these maps helped me see how location adds another layer to the story. The household maps show how the same locations can be understood through water samples, health reports and relocation. The regional map connects Hinkley to the Los Angeles area and gives a sense of the distances involved in Erin’s investigation.
